justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level for the underlying asset at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 573.5 was anchored closely to the last observed price, with only a small positive drift reflecting the slight bullish momentum visible in recent trading sessions and the tendency for mean reversion to be weak over very short horizons. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 576, reflecting the continuation of a mild upward trend while acknowledging that weekly price action tends to be dominated by short-term sentiment and macro data releases. At one month, the estimate of 580 reflects a longer-term drift assumption, incorporating the general tendency of risk assets to appreciate modestly over time when no strong bearish catalyst is present.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect typical realized volatility scaling with the square root of time. At one day, the interval of 558 to 589 represents roughly a ±2.7% range, consistent with moderate daily volatility. By one week, the interval widens to 548–604, and by one month it expands further to 528–635, capturing the accumulating uncertainty from multiple trading sessions and the greater potential for macro or fundamental news to compound. I also factored in that short-term options markets tend to price in somewhat elevated implied volatility relative to realized volatility, which informed the width choices at the longer horizons.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a hotter-than-expected inflation print triggering aggressive central bank rhetoric, or a sudden credit event — could produce a sharp selloff well beyond the lower bound. Geopolitical escalation or a liquidity shock in financial markets could similarly produce fat-tail moves. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from a major central bank, strong earnings beats, or a short-squeeze dynamic in heavily shorted names could drive prices significantly above the upper bound, particularly at the one-month horizon where more time exists for such catalysts to develop.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively normal market conditions and do not fully account for discontinuous jump risk or structural breaks. In practice, tail events — whether a sudden regulatory announcement, unexpected geopolitical development, or a black swan macro shock — occur more frequently than a simple Gaussian volatility model would suggest. Readers should treat the 90% confidence intervals as reasonable central ranges rather than hard boundaries, and recognize that the true distribution of outcomes has heavier tails than my stated intervals imply.
